title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's May 16, 2010 Inquirer column hailing the Noynoy Aquino landslide as a 'thunderous triumph of People Power' that survived 'sweltering kilometric queues, technical glitches... and other booboos of Comelec and Smartmatic'

His framing of a new, third genre of People Power -- 'of the strict constitutional genre' -- contrasting the 'extra constitutional' People Power 1 (Cory's 1986 revolutionary ascent) and the 'intra constitutional' but contested People Power 2 (GMA in 2001) with the 'unquestioned constitutionality' of Noynoy's 2010 mandate

His catalogue of the avoidable failures -- clustered precincts with 'one... BEI and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters,' wasted votes from malfunctions, weak training, and 'small covers' that violated ballot secrecy (the Inquirer photo of Estrada's exposed ballot)

His warning about the count's opacity -- that the celebrated 'instant transmission' and parallel counts all came 'from the same election returns spewed out by the PCOS machines,' with 'no check on how the machines tallied' individual ballots after Comelec 'disengaged a machine safeguard'
sub_topics: The triumph: despite 'sweltering kilometric queues, technical glitches, carelessness, mismanagement, and other booboos,' the people 'persevered,' and 'human frailties and technological hitches could not stop the thunderous Noynoy landslide'

A new genre of People Power: the first nationwide automated election was 'a resounding triumph of People Power of the strict constitutional genre' -- the people choosing a peaceful transition 'no longer by staging mammoth street rallies, but by pouring a massive electoral mandate'

The three People Powers: People Power 1 was 'extra constitutional' (Cory's 1986 government 'revolutionary in character'); People Power 2 was, per Estrada v. Desierto (2001), 'intra constitutional,' though 'many constitutionalists still contest' GMA's 2001 legitimacy; and People Power 3 (2010) 'catapults Noynoy with unquestioned constitutionality' -- fittingly embodied in 'the 1987 Constitution of Cory'
The mandate's clout: the 'thunderous landslide' gave Noynoy 'a clear head start' and 'enormous clout to transform our savaged democratic institutions immediately'

The clustering fiasco: as CJP had predicted, clustering 'precipitated long lines... caused mainly by the logistical miscalculation of assigning only one Board of Election Inspectors (BEI) and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters' -- he and his wife waited 45 minutes (luckier than many, including Noynoy, who 'sweated many hours'), and how many were 'actually disenfranchised... may never be accurately counted'

Wasted and uncounted votes: votes lost to 'PCOS machine malfunction, oval misalignment, ballot rejection, and printing errors,' plus the effects of weak BEI training, thin instructions, scanty voter education, and voter-list exclusions, 'may no longer be precisely known' -- puzzles CJP agrees with Sen. Jamby Madrigal 'must still be investigated'

Secrecy violated: among 'glaring errors,' the Comelec chose 'small covers measuring only half the size of the ballots,' violating vote secrecy -- epitomized by 'the Inquirer front-page photo' catching Estrada's ballot and his failure to vote for a VP -- and lacked privacy booths, unlike past Comelecs

No transparency of the precinct count: the applauded 'instant transmission' and the PPCRV, GMA7 and ABS-CBN parallel counts all drew 'from the same election returns spewed out by the PCOS machines,' so they 'do not explain how the PCOS machines counted the individual votes' -- with 'no check' on the tally after the Comelec 'inexplicably disengaged' a safeguard that would have let voters confirm an on-screen report before counting; still, CJP 'heave[s] a sigh of relief' that nationwide failure, source-code corruption, holdover and military rule 'did not come to pass'

institutions: the Commission on Elections and Smartmatic

events: the May 10, 2010 first nationwide automated election and the Noynoy landslide

stances.claim: The 2010 election was 'a resounding triumph of People Power of the strict constitutional genre' -- a third, fully constitutional People Power (against the 'extra constitutional' 1986 and the contested 'intra constitutional' 2001) that gave Noynoy 'unquestioned constitutionality' and clout to reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: typology-and-elevation: situating 2010 as the legitimate culmination of three People Powers

stances.claim: Many failures were avoidable -- the clustering that put 'one... BEI and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters,' wasted votes, weak training, and 'small covers' that violated ballot secrecy -- and the resulting disenfranchisement 'must still be investigated.'
stances.rhetorical_move: praise-with-accountability: crediting the result while itemizing preventable lapses

stances.claim: The count lacked transparency: all the celebrated transmissions and parallel counts came 'from the same election returns,' with 'no check on how the machines tallied' individual ballots after Comelec disengaged a confirmation safeguard -- though the worst-case scenarios mercifully 'did not come to pass.'
stances.rhetorical_move: caveat-amid-relief: flagging the opacity even while celebrating the outcome

notable_anecdotes: 45 minutes, and lucky: CJP recounts that he and his wife, arriving before 7 a.m. with 20 ahead, voted after 45 minutes -- luckier than Noynoy and others who 'sweated many hours.'
Estrada's exposed ballot: he cites the Inquirer front-page photo that caught Estrada's ballot (and his failure to vote for VP) as proof the half-size covers violated secrecy.
Counts from one source: he notes the PPCRV, GMA7 and ABS-CBN parallel counts all drew 'from the same election returns,' so none verified how the PCOS tallied individual votes.
A disengaged safeguard: he flags that the Comelec 'inexplicably disengaged' a feature that would have flashed a vote report for voters to confirm before counting.
target_audience: Citizens celebrating -- and scrutinizing -- the automated result
decision_framework_signals: a-decisive-mandate enables reform and deters mischief
count-transparency: a machine tally needs a verifiable check
one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 16, 2010 Inquirer column, hails the Noynoy Aquino landslide as a 'thunderous triumph of People Power' that survived 'sweltering kilometric queues, technical glitches... and other booboos of Comelec and Smartmatic.' The first nationwide automated election, he writes, was 'People Power of the strict constitutional genre' -- the people choosing a peaceful transition 'no longer by staging mammoth street rallies, but by pouring a massive electoral mandate.' He sets it among three: the 'extra constitutional' People Power 1 (Cory's 1986 revolutionary ascent), the 'intra constitutional' but contested People Power 2 (GMA in 2001, per Estrada v. Desierto), and now People Power 3, which 'catapults Noynoy with unquestioned constitutionality' and is fittingly embodied in 'the 1987 Constitution of Cory.' Yet he itemizes avoidable failures: the clustering that, as he had predicted, assigned 'only one... BEI and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters' (he and his wife waited 45 minutes; Noynoy 'sweated many hours'); wasted votes from 'PCOS machine malfunction, oval misalignment, ballot rejection, and printing errors'; weak training and voter-list exclusions; and 'small covers... half the size of the ballots' that violated secrecy -- captured by the Inquirer photo of Estrada's exposed ballot -- disenfranchisement that, he agrees with Sen. Jamby Madrigal, 'must still be investigated.' He also warns that the celebrated 'instant transmission' and the PPCRV, GMA7 and ABS-CBN parallel counts all drew 'from the same election returns spewed out by the PCOS machines,' so none explained 'how the PCOS machines counted the individual votes,' leaving 'no check on how the machines tallied' after the Comelec 'inexplicably disengaged' a voter-confirmation safeguard. Still, he 'heave[s] a sigh of relief' that nationwide failure, source-code corruption, holdover and military rule 'did not come to pass,' hailing 'the miraculous start of a peaceful transition of power.'
